---
title: "Agent-Friendly CLI Design"
subtitle: "Designing a command-line tool that an autonomous agent can drive as reliably as a human can"
---

**Framing.** A command-line tool used to have exactly one operator: a person at a
terminal, reading prose output and deciding what to type next. Agentic systems add
a second operator with very different needs — an LLM that *spawns* the process,
*parses* its output, and *branches* on the result without a human in the loop. A
CLI that was only ever designed for the first operator tends to fail the second in
quiet, maddening ways: it prints a pretty table the agent can't parse, it blocks on
an interactive prompt nobody answers, or it returns exit code `0` while printing
`error:` to stdout.

The **agent-friendly CLI** is the discipline of treating that second operator as a
first-class consumer. The clearest worked example I've found is the design doc for
**clickclack**, the CLI/server from the OpenClaw ecosystem
([`docs/agent-friendly-cli.md`](https://github.com/openclaw/clickclack/blob/main/docs/agent-friendly-cli.md)).
This chapter pulls the durable principles out of that doc, connects them to the
pre-agentic CLI-design canon, and ends with a reusable contract you can drop into
any repo.

---

## 1. What changes when the operator is an LLM

Most of what makes a CLI pleasant for a human also makes it usable for an agent —
the agent-era guidelines are largely the [clig.dev Command Line Interface
Guidelines](https://clig.dev) and the "12-Factor CLI" ideas **re-derived under one
extra constraint: the operator cannot improvise.** A human reading `error: channel
"ops" not found, did you mean "op"?` self-corrects instantly. An agent reading the
same string has to be *prompted* to parse it, might hallucinate a fix, and has no
stable signal to branch on.

So the shift is less "invent new rules" and more "stop relying on human
adaptability." Concretely:

| Human operator tolerates | Agent operator needs instead |
|---|---|
| Prose output, pretty tables, colour | A declared machine format (`--json`, `--plain`) |
| Reading the error message to decide | A **stable exit code** to branch on |
| Answering an interactive prompt | `--no-input` and stdin-driven input |
| "It usually reconnects if I re-run it" | Durable cursor recovery, no lost events |
| Mixed stdout/stderr they can eyeball | stdout = data only; stderr = everything else |

The rest of the chapter is those five rows, made concrete.

---

## 2. The six pillars

### 2.1 A stable machine-output contract

The default output stays human-friendly (`sent msg_01kr… to #ops`). The contract
is that a machine format is always *one flag away* and never requires parsing prose:

- `--json` → a **single JSON object** for finite commands.
- `--json` on a **stream** → **newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON)**, one event per
  line, flushed as it happens.
- `--plain` → stable, column-stable, ANSI-free lines for `awk`/`cut`-style consumers.

```json
// finite command, --json
{"message":{"id":"msg_01kr...","channel_id":"chn_...","body":"hello"}}

// streaming command, --json  (one self-describing object per line)
{"type":"message.created","cursor":"evt_...","message":{"id":"msg_..."}}
```

The detail that earns its keep: each streamed object **carries its own
`cursor`/`type`** — the stream is self-describing, so a consumer that reconnects
knows exactly where it is. (More on that in §2.6.)

### 2.2 stdout is data; stderr is everything else

This is the single most violated rule and the one agents punish hardest. The
clickclack rule is absolute: **only the requested result goes to stdout**;
diagnostics, warnings, reconnection notices, and `--verbose` all go to **stderr**.

```
agent-summarize incident.log | clickclack threads reply msg_01kr... --stdin
                                         │
                  stdout ───────────────►│  clean JSON/text the agent parses
                  stderr ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ┘  "reconnecting…", warnings, debug
```

If a "reconnecting…" notice lands in stdout, every downstream `jq` breaks. Keeping
the channels disjoint is what makes the tool safe to pipe.

### 2.3 Exit codes are the control-flow contract

> *Scripts should branch on codes, not error messages.*

clickclack assigns distinct codes to distinct failure classes:

| Code | Meaning | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Success | 5 | Authenticated but unauthorized |
| 1 | Generic failure | 10 | Network unavailable |
| 2 | Invalid usage / validation | 11 | Server returned unexpected response |
| 3 | Auth required / invalid | | |
| 4 | Resource not found | | |

The payoff is that an agent can write *real* control flow — "retry on 10, re-auth on
3, give up on 2" — without ever reading a sentence. Error **messages** are for the
human; exit **codes** are the machine API. Both must exist; neither substitutes for
the other.

### 2.4 Never block waiting for a human

An agent that hits an interactive prompt hangs forever. Two mechanisms prevent it:

- `--no-input` disables every prompt; the command proceeds or fails with a code.
- A documented **input precedence** so the body can come from wherever the caller
  has it: positional arg → `--body <text>` → `--file <path>` → `--stdin`.

```sh
clickclack send "hello from a script"                       # positional
clickclack messages send --channel ops --file incident.md   # from a file
printf 'build passed\n' | clickclack send --stdin            # from a pipe
```

stdin support is what makes the tool a good Unix citizen — it composes with
whatever produced the text upstream (a log, another agent, a heredoc).

### 2.5 Configuration resolves in a documented order

Predictability beats cleverness. clickclack resolves config highest-to-lowest:

```
1. CLI flags             --server / --token / --channel ...   (most explicit)
2. Environment variables CLICKCLACK_SERVER, CLICKCLACK_TOKEN
3. User config file      ~/.config/clickclack/config.json
4. Built-in defaults     localhost:8080                       (least explicit)
```

An agent can set everything via env vars for one invocation and override a single
value with a flag, with zero ambiguity about which wins. Note also that credentials
are **scoped to the server** they belong to — a token for one endpoint is never
leaked to another, which matters the moment an agent talks to both localhost and a
hosted server in the same session.

### 2.6 Long-running streams must be durably recoverable

This is the pillar most CLIs skip, and the one that separates "demo" from
"production agent infrastructure." Streaming commands (`messages tail`, `watch`,
`events tail`) survive restarts:

```
            ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 restart ──►│ 1. load saved cursor                          │
            │      ~/.local/state/clickclack/cursors/       │
            │ 2. GET /api/realtime/events?after_cursor=...   │  ← replay the gap
            │ 3. open WebSocket /api/realtime/ws             │  ← go live
            │ 4. persist cursor after EACH event            │  ← never lose place
            │ 5. on `resync_required` → refetch state        │  ← self-heal
            └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Because every event carries its cursor (§2.1) and the cursor is persisted after each
one, an agent watcher that crashes and respawns loses **no** events and produces **no**
duplicates-by-default. That is the property that lets you trust an agent to babysit a
channel for days.

## 3. The clickclack command surface, briefly

The doc also models a clean command taxonomy worth imitating — verbs grouped by
domain rather than a flat soup:

```
server      serve · migrate · backup · export
auth        login · logout · whoami · status
workspace   workspaces list/use · channels list/use/create
messaging   send · messages send/list/tail/watch · threads open/reply
            reactions add/remove · events tail
```

with global flags (`--server`, `--workspace`, `--channel`, `--token`, `--json`,
`--plain`, `--no-input`, `--verbose`, `--no-color`) that apply uniformly. Uniformity
is itself an agent-friendliness property: an agent that learns the flag convention
once can apply it to every subcommand.

A representative end-to-end agent usage:

```sh
# stream a channel as JSON, non-interactively, against a hosted server
CLICKCLACK_SERVER=https://clickclack.chat \
CLICKCLACK_TOKEN=ses_... \
clickclack messages tail --channel ops --json --no-input

# CI branching purely on success/failure
if pnpm test; then
  clickclack send --channel builds "tests passed"
else
  clickclack send --channel builds "tests failed"
fi
```

---

## 5. Takeaways

- An agent is a **second operator** with a stricter contract than a human: it can't
  improvise around prose, prompts, or ambiguous failures.
- The contract is mostly the **pre-agentic CLI canon** (clig.dev, 12-factor CLI)
  enforced rigorously — plus one genuinely new requirement: **durable stream
  recovery** for long-running watchers.
- Keep the two interfaces layered, not forked: human-readable by default, machine
  output one flag away, exit codes as the real API.
- Reuse the §4 contract as a checklist; an agent can self-audit any CLI against it.
